length.text: Tiny: about 5 to 10 cm, rarely 15 cm

reproduction.text: Lays eggs; all are females (no males needed)

overview.text: The Brahminy Blind Snake is a tiny, harmless burrowing snake that looks just like an earthworm. It has spread around the world in the soil of potted plants, so it is sometimes called the 'flowerpot snake'.

identification.text: Shiny, very thin and worm-like, charcoal-grey to silver-grey or beige. The head and tail look almost the same; the eyes are tiny dots under the scales, and the tail ends in a small spine. Unlike an earthworm it has scales, not rings.

size.label: Adults
size.text: Usually about 5 to 10 cm (2 to 4 in) long, rarely up to about 15 cm.

distribution.label: Native
distribution.text: Probably originally from Africa and Asia.

distribution.label: Introduced
distribution.text: Carried by people to many other parts of the world, including Australia, the Americas and the Pacific islands.

behaviour.text: Spends nearly its whole life underground, burrowing in soil and leaf litter.

reproduction.text: Lays eggs. Every known individual is female: the females produce young without males (parthenogenesis). It may be the only snake that always reproduces this way.

funfacts.text: No male Brahminy Blind Snake has ever been found - mothers have daughters all on their own.

recognise.text: Looks like a shiny earthworm with scales.
Head and tail look almost the same.
